title: Radio interview, one host and two guests, with short interjections

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Welcome back to Field Notes. Today we're talking about listening to the ocean floor. With me are Dr. Samuel Achebe, an oceanographer at the Bergen Institute, and Mei Lin Tan, who builds sensor systems at Cobalt Marine. Welcome to you both.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Thanks for having us, Elena.

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Happy to be here.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Samuel, let's start with the big idea. Why would anyone put a microphone, essentially, on the bottom of the Atlantic?

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Because the ocean is full of information that never reaches land. Earthquakes, ships, whale calls, even storms two thousand kilometres away. A single hydrophone can pick up all of it, and sound travels about 1,500 metres per second in water, almost five times faster than in air.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Five times.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Roughly, yes.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Mei Lin, where do you come in?

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: I build the hardware that survives down there. At 4,000 metres the pressure is about 400 times what you feel at the surface, so every housing, every connector, every seal has to be designed for that.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: And how long does it have to last?

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Twenty-five years, ideally, without anyone touching it. A repair vessel costs around $60,000 a day, so reliability is the whole business case.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Which is why we piggyback on telecom cables.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Explain that for listeners.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Transatlantic cables already carry repeaters every 80 kilometres or so. If we add sensors at those repeaters, we get a sensor network for the price of a few extra components rather than a whole new cable.

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: The programme is called SMART cables, short for Science Monitoring And Reliable Telecommunications, and it's backed by a joint task force of three United Nations agencies.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: What does a sensor actually measure?

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Three things: temperature, pressure, and acceleration. From those we derive sea level, seabed motion, and the arrival time of seismic waves.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: And that last one is the prize. An earthquake early warning system on land gets maybe ten seconds. A sensor 100 kilometres offshore can buy you more than a minute.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: A minute is a lot.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: It's enough to stop a train.

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Or open a fire station door.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Okay, but how accurate is that warning?

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Accurate enough to be useful, not accurate enough to be certain. The first few seconds give you the location and a rough magnitude, say 6.5 plus or minus 0.5. The estimate improves as more of the wave train arrives.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Plus or minus half a magnitude is a big error bar.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: It is. But a magnitude 6 and a magnitude 7 both justify stopping the trains.

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Fair enough.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Mei Lin, what goes wrong?

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Everything, eventually. Fishing trawlers drag anchors across cables, about 150 faults a year worldwide. Sharks have bitten cables, which sounds like a joke, but we've seen the teeth marks.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: I'd love to see that.

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: I'll send you a photo.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: What about maintenance? You said nobody touches it.

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: We design for it. Each node has redundant power supplies, and the firmware can be updated through the cable itself, so we never need to go down there to fix a software bug.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: That's the part people underestimate. Firmware over a 6,000 kilometre link, with a round trip of about 80 milliseconds.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Eighty milliseconds.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Plus the repeaters.

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Exactly.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Samuel, with all those sensors, how do you handle the data? It sounds like a firehose.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: It is. One station produces about 200 gigabytes a day. We process it near the shore using a model trained on twelve years of recordings from the Azores array, and flag anything unusual within seconds.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Unusual meaning?

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: A magnitude 4 earthquake, a ship engine we don't recognise, or a whale doing something new.

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Mm-hm.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: How do you know a sensor hasn't drifted?

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Pressure sensors drift. A quartz gauge, the kind we use, drifts by about 1 millibar a year. We cross-check against tide gauges on shore, and against the neighbouring node 80 kilometres away.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: A tsunami is the best calibration there is. You see a clean 20 centimetre wave pass node after node, and any outlier stands out immediately.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Has that happened?

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Last winter a small tsunami, about 30 centimetres, crossed the array, and every node saw it within a second of the prediction.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Let me ask a hard question. Who pays for this?

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Right now, governments and research grants. Cobalt Marine's contract with the Norwegian Research Council is worth about 14 million kroner over three years.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: And telecom companies are starting to see the value in it. If a cable is cut, a sensor tells them where within a kilometre.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: So it pays for itself?

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Eventually.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Eventually.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: If this works, could we cover the whole ocean?

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Not the whole ocean. The cables follow trade routes, so the Southern Ocean is mostly silent. We'd get the North Atlantic, the Mediterranean, and the Pacific rim.

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Roughly 1.4 million kilometres of cable exist today.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: And how many of them carry sensors?

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Almost none. A handful of test segments.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Which is the opportunity.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Okay. Last round, quick answers. Biggest surprise in the data?

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Whales singing in the same key as the cable hum.

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Honestly, how quiet it is at 3 a.m.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Biggest fear?

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: A budget cut in year four.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Same.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: One thing you want listeners to do?

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Ask your national government whether it supports SMART cables.

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: And thank a cable engineer.

turns.speaker: elena
turns.text: Dr. Samuel Achebe and Mei Lin Tan, thank you both.

turns.speaker: samuel
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: meilin
turns.text: Thanks, Elena.
